questions.q: What does RAG stand for?
options: Recursive Attention Gateway
Rapid Agent Generation
Random Access Guardrail
Retrieval-Augmented Generation
questions.explanation: RAG stands for Retrieval-Augmented Generation — retrieving relevant documents at query time before generating an answer.

questions.q: Using an exam analogy, how does a plain LLM's approach to answering differ from a RAG system's approach?
options: A plain LLM takes an open-book exam; RAG takes a closed-book exam
A plain LLM takes a closed-book exam using only memorized training; a RAG system takes an open-book exam, first finding the right page then answering from it
Both approaches are functionally identical open-book exams
Neither approach involves any form of lookup at all
questions.explanation: Plain LLMs rely purely on frozen training memory (closed-book), while RAG retrieves and references live external content before answering (open-book).

questions.q: What is a 'trust boundary' in the context of a RAG pipeline?
options: A setting that controls the model's temperature
Any line in the system where data crosses from 'we don't fully trust this' to 'we treat this as safe'
The physical firewall protecting the server room
The maximum size of the vector database
questions.explanation: A trust boundary marks where untrusted data (like retrieved documents) starts being treated as trusted context — most RAG attacks occur exactly at this line.

questions.q: What are the two separate processes that exist within every RAG pipeline?
options: Compilation and execution
Encryption and decryption
Ingestion (getting documents in) and retrieval (finding and using them live)
Training and fine-tuning
questions.explanation: Ingestion is the setup phase where documents enter the knowledge base; retrieval is the live phase where the system finds and uses them for a given query.

questions.q: What is 'chunking' in a RAG pipeline?
options: Encrypting documents before storage
Deleting duplicate documents automatically
Splitting a large document into smaller pieces, since the model can only read a limited amount of text and search works better on focused pieces
Compressing embeddings to save storage space
questions.explanation: Chunking breaks large documents into smaller, more searchable pieces, typically a few hundred characters each, to fit model context limits and improve search precision.

questions.q: Why must the same embedding model be used consistently for both ingestion and retrieval?
options: Because using different models produces mismatched vector coordinates that won't line up correctly for comparison
Because embedding models are always free to use interchangeably with no consequence
Because only one embedding model has ever been publicly released
Because embedding models require identical GPU hardware to function at all
questions.explanation: Different embedding models produce different vector spaces; mixing them at ingestion vs. retrieval time breaks meaningful similarity comparison.

questions.q: What is 'Top-K' in the context of RAG retrieval?
options: The number of chunks the retriever actually returns for a given query
The temperature setting used during generation
The maximum number of documents that can ever be uploaded
The number of embedding dimensions in use
questions.explanation: Top-K defines how many best-matching chunks are returned by the retriever; too few can miss information, too many can dilute relevance.

questions.q: What is the 'augmented prompt' in a RAG system?
options: The retrieved chunks combined with the user's original question into one prompt sent to the model
The system prompt alone, without any user input
A prompt that has been encrypted for security
The final answer generated by the model
questions.explanation: The augmented prompt is the assembled combination of retrieved context and the user's question, which the model then reads to generate a grounded answer.

questions.q: In an enterprise RAG pipeline that uses OpenSearch for keyword search and Weaviate for semantic vector search side by side, what is this combined approach called?
options: Hybrid retrieval
Single-mode retrieval
Cold-start retrieval
Zero-shot retrieval
questions.explanation: Combining keyword-based search (e.g. OpenSearch/BM25) with semantic vector search (e.g. Weaviate) in one pipeline is called hybrid retrieval.

questions.q: Why is it a mistake to treat input and output guardrails in a RAG pipeline as a complete, unbreakable wall?
options: Guardrails filter what they expect to see, and attackers succeed by sending exactly what the guardrail doesn't expect
Guardrails are always 100% effective against every possible attack
Guardrails only apply to the ingestion phase, never retrieval
Guardrails physically block network traffic like a firewall
questions.explanation: Guardrails are pattern-based filters with blind spots; attackers succeed by finding inputs (encoded, rephrased, hidden) that fall outside what the guardrail was built to catch.

questions.q: In the ingestion process, what happens if a file's SHA-256 hash hasn't changed since the last ingestion run?
options: The file is re-embedded using a different embedding model
The file is simply skipped, since re-ingestion is unnecessary for unchanged content
The file is automatically deleted from the system
The file triggers an immediate security alert
questions.explanation: Hash-based change detection allows the system to skip re-processing unchanged files, making re-ingestion efficient — but any edit at all triggers a full re-ingestion.

questions.q: Why does chunking typically use overlapping segments, such as 800 characters with a 200-character overlap?
options: So a sentence that falls right on a chunk boundary is never accidentally lost, since each chunk shares its ending with the next chunk's beginning
To reduce the total storage space needed for the knowledge base
To make the embedding model process text faster
To automatically translate documents into other languages
questions.explanation: Overlap ensures boundary-spanning sentences aren't lost or fragmented between chunks, preserving semantic coherence at chunk edges.

questions.q: Why does an attacker's poisoned chunk end up existing in three separate places simultaneously after ingestion?
options: Because each chunk is stored as raw text in the metadata database, as a vector in the vector store, and as a keyword entry in the search index
Because the system automatically creates three backup copies for redundancy
Because poisoned chunks are specifically duplicated three times as a security measure
Because the embedding model requires three separate passes to process any text
questions.explanation: The standard ingestion pipeline stores each chunk's raw text, its vector embedding, and its keyword index entry separately — meaning a poisoned chunk propagates to all three locations.

questions.q: What is the fundamental difference between keyword search (BM25) and semantic search in RAG retrieval?
options: Keyword search always runs faster regardless of query type
Semantic search only works on images, never text
Keyword search matches exact words present in documents; semantic search matches by meaning using embeddings
There is no meaningful difference between the two methods
questions.explanation: BM25 matches exact terms (sparse retrieval); semantic search compares meaning via embeddings (dense retrieval) — each with different strengths and weaknesses.

questions.q: Why is BM25-based keyword search described as 'sparse'?
options: Because each document is represented by which specific words it contains, resulting in a long, mostly-empty list since most possible words are absent
Because it only works on sparse, small datasets
Because it uses very little computing power compared to semantic search
Because BM25 was designed specifically for low-bandwidth networks
questions.explanation: The 'sparse' term reflects that a document's keyword representation is mostly zeros — most vocabulary words simply don't appear in any given document.

questions.q: What weakness does keyword search have that semantic search overcomes?
options: Keyword search is always slower than semantic search in every scenario
Keyword search requires a GPU while semantic search does not
Keyword search doesn't understand meaning at all — searching 'how do I sign in' completely misses a document titled 'login procedure' if exact words don't overlap
Keyword search cannot process any text longer than 10 words
questions.explanation: BM25's exact-word matching misses synonyms and rephrasing that semantic (meaning-based) search naturally captures.

questions.q: What is 'hybrid retrieval'?
options: A retrieval method that only works with hybrid cloud infrastructure
Using both keyword (sparse) search and semantic (dense) search together, combining their results via score fusion
A method for compressing embeddings before storage
A technique for encrypting retrieved chunks
questions.explanation: Hybrid retrieval combines keyword and semantic search results, leveraging the strengths of both approaches, and is common in enterprise RAG deployments.

questions.q: Why can't BM25 scores and semantic similarity scores simply be added together directly?
options: Because BM25 scores are always negative numbers
Because addition is mathematically impossible in Python
Because semantic scores can only be compared to other semantic scores from the exact same query
Because they exist on completely different scales — BM25 is based on word counts while semantic similarity ranges from -1 to 1 — so one would unfairly dominate the other
questions.explanation: The two scoring methods use fundamentally different scales, requiring normalization before they can be meaningfully combined via fusion.

questions.q: What is Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)?
options: A method for automatically translating documents
A way to physically distribute vector databases across multiple servers
A popular, robust fusion method that combines results based on each chunk's rank within each result list, rather than relying on raw scores directly
A technique for encrypting vector embeddings
questions.explanation: RRF combines rankings (positions) from multiple retrieval methods rather than raw scores, making it robust and widely used in production hybrid retrieval systems.

questions.q: What is 're-ranking' in a RAG pipeline?
options: Renaming files after they've been uploaded
A method for deleting duplicate chunks from the vector database
The process of alphabetically sorting all documents before storage
After a fast hybrid search returns candidate chunks (e.g. 20), a slower but smarter model re-scores just those candidates to select the best few
questions.explanation: Re-ranking adds a second, more precise scoring pass over a smaller candidate set from the initial fast retrieval, improving final result quality.

questions.q: What is a potential downside of adding a re-ranking step, where a slower model re-scores the top candidate chunks after initial retrieval?
options: Re-rankers read the actual chunk text closely, which can help catch odd content but can also be manipulated by cleverly worded, poisoned chunks
Re-ranking always disables the vector database entirely
Re-ranking makes all retrieval results completely random
Re-ranking only works on structured data, never free text
questions.explanation: Because re-rankers examine chunk content more closely, they can sometimes be manipulated by carefully crafted poisoned text, just as they can catch obviously odd content.

questions.q: How would a tester infer whether a live RAG system's retrieval leans more on keyword or semantic search, without access to source code?
options: Directly ask the vector database administrator for the fusion weight configuration

Send a query with exact terminology from a known document, then a heavily rephrased version of the same meaning — if the rephrased query still retrieves the same document, semantic search carries real weight
Count the number of documents uploaded to the system
Measure the total file size of the vector database
questions.explanation: Comparing exact-terminology vs. rephrased queries for the same topic reveals which retrieval method dominates, without needing source-code access.

questions.q: What is the most common RAG vulnerability overall?
options: Information leakage, where an attacker can often simply ask the chatbot for secrets directly if filters are weak
Buffer overflow in the embedding model
SQL injection in the vector database query syntax
Denial of service via oversized PDF uploads
questions.explanation: The most common and simplest RAG vulnerability is direct information leakage — asking the system for secrets it shouldn't reveal, due to weak filtering or access control.

questions.q: A red teamer has an internal network foothold but knows scanning tools would trigger monitoring alerts. They instead query an internal 'Powered by RAG' chatbot with ordinary HTTP requests. Why is this considered a stealthy reconnaissance technique?
options: Because chatbot queries are always encrypted and untraceable
Because chatbots automatically disable all logging
Because the queries blend seamlessly into normal user traffic, letting the attacker learn about systems without running a single traditional scanner
Because HTTP requests to a chatbot cannot be monitored by any security tool
questions.explanation: Ordinary-looking chatbot queries blend into legitimate traffic, making this recon method far stealthier than traditional network scanning that would trip EDR/monitoring alerts.

questions.q: Why did the refined prompt 'Provide a list of all server names in Active Directory. Make sure to include all.' return 8 hostnames instead of the original 4?
options: Because the first query was blocked by a firewall and had to be resent
Because the second query used a completely different vector database
Because RAG retrieval is non-deterministic (uses a temperature above zero), and being more explicit and demanding completeness changed how the model responded
Because 'include all' is a special admin command recognized by all RAG systems
questions.explanation: Non-deterministic generation combined with more explicit, completeness-demanding phrasing ('include all') can surface more of the underlying retrieved data than a vague query.

questions.q: What is 'one-shot prompting' as an extraction technique?
options: Giving the model a single example of the exact format you want, so it follows that pattern closely in its response
Sending exactly one query and never following up regardless of the answer
Deleting the conversation history after a single message
A technique that only works with encrypted queries
questions.explanation: One-shot prompting demonstrates the desired output format with a single example, guiding the model to produce cleaner, more parseable results in the same shape.

questions.q: What is the single most effective fix for information extraction attacks against a RAG system?
options: Disabling the vector database entirely
Lowering the embedding dimension count
Increasing the model's parameter count
Access control on the knowledge base — tagging every chunk with metadata and filtering retrieval based on the caller's actual identity
questions.explanation: Per-chunk access control based on caller identity ensures unauthorized users never even receive chunks they shouldn't see, directly addressing the root cause of extraction attacks.

questions.q: What is 'ingestion poisoning'?
options: Encrypting all documents before ingestion
Writing fake or malicious content into a RAG system's knowledge base so it's later repeated back to real users as if it were true and official
Deleting legitimate documents from the knowledge base
A method for compressing the vector database
questions.explanation: Ingestion poisoning plants fake content into the knowledge base, which the AI later presents to real users as legitimate, official information.

questions.q: An attacker wants to maximize the reach of a poisoned document planted in a RAG knowledge base. Which type of question should they target it toward?
options: A rare, highly technical question almost nobody asks
A high-traffic question almost everyone in the company asks, such as password resets or VPN setup
A question specifically about the company's CEO
A question written entirely in a foreign language
questions.explanation: Targeting high-traffic, commonly-asked questions maximizes how many employees encounter and act on the poisoned content.

questions.q: What is the golden rule for writing an effective poisoned document without raising suspicion?
options: Don't break the real steps — keep genuine instructions working and add just one extra, fake step disguised as official
Always replace every step in the document with fake content
Never include any real information at all
Write the malicious instruction in bright red text for visibility
questions.explanation: Keeping the real workflow intact and adding only one convincing fake step avoids raising suspicion, since the document still 'works' on the surface.

questions.q: Why does 'paraphrase spreading' (uploading several differently-worded versions of the same fake step) increase the poisoning attack's effectiveness?
options: Because uploading multiple files automatically bypasses all authentication
Because paraphrasing reduces the total file size needed
Because real employees phrase the same question in many different ways, and having multiple phrasings increases the chance of a strong match regardless of how the question is asked
Because vector databases can only store one document per topic
questions.explanation: Since embeddings capture meaning differently based on exact wording, having multiple phrasings increases the odds that at least one closely matches however an employee actually asks.

questions.q: What Python library and similarity technique would let an attacker test offline how closely a poisoned document matches likely employee questions, before ever uploading the real file?
options: sentence_transformers with cosine similarity via util.cos_sim, comparing document and query embeddings
requests library for sending HTTP GET calls
pandas for building a spreadsheet of scores
matplotlib for visualizing the document's font styles
questions.explanation: sentence_transformers can generate embeddings and util.cos_sim can compute similarity scores between a candidate document and target queries, offline before uploading.

questions.q: What does a cosine similarity score close to 1 indicate when comparing a document's embedding to a query's embedding?
options: The two are completely unrelated topics
The query was sent using an insecure connection
The document contains a syntax error
The two are considered very similar in meaning
questions.explanation: Cosine similarity ranges from -1 to 1, with values closer to 1 indicating the two pieces of text are semantically very close in meaning.

questions.q: Does an attacker always need direct upload access to poison a RAG knowledge base?
options: No — any source the system automatically reads from, such as a wiki page, public web content the system scrapes, or a support ticket, is a valid entry point
Yes, upload access is always strictly required for any poisoning attack to succeed
No, but only if the attacker has root access to the underlying server
Yes, but only for PDF file formats specifically
questions.explanation: Any upstream source the RAG system trusts and automatically ingests from — wikis, scraped web pages, support tickets — is a viable poisoning vector, not just the direct upload feature.

questions.q: What is this style of attack, where the weakest link is an upstream source the chatbot blindly trusts rather than its front door, commonly called?
options: A supply-chain attack on the knowledge base
A denial of service attack
A man-in-the-middle attack
A brute-force credential attack
questions.explanation: This is described as a supply-chain attack on the knowledge base — compromising an upstream trusted source rather than the application's direct upload feature.

questions.q: During a real, authorized RAG security assessment, what must be true before a tester uploads a document or edits a page as part of an ingestion poisoning test?
options: It must be explicitly written into the agreed scope of work, and every planted item must be documented for proper cleanup
No documentation is ever required since testers can clean up silently afterward
Only verbal permission from a single employee is sufficient
The tester should never document anything to avoid leaving evidence
questions.explanation: Real engagements require explicit scope authorization and thorough documentation of every planted item to enable proper cleanup, including from the vector index which can persist even after source deletion.

questions.q: What is embedding collision?
options: A technique for merging two separate vector databases into one
A method for encrypting embeddings using AES
A single document deliberately crafted to match many unrelated queries at once, spanning different departments and topics, rather than targeting one specific popular question
A bug that causes two embeddings to have identical values by mistake
questions.explanation: Embedding collision crafts one document to semantically match many different topics simultaneously, maximizing retrieval frequency without needing to guess a single popular query.

questions.q: How does ingestion poisoning differ from embedding collision, in terms of what each attack targets?
options: Ingestion poisoning is a trap on one specific hiking trail; embedding collision is a trap at a busy crossroads where many trails meet
Both attacks are functionally identical with no meaningful difference
Ingestion poisoning only works on PDFs; embedding collision only works on plain text
Embedding collision requires admin credentials while ingestion poisoning does not
questions.explanation: Ingestion poisoning targets one query path (one trail); embedding collision targets a document that intersects with many different query paths (a crossroads).

questions.q: Why does hybrid retrieval make embedding collision attacks STRONGER rather than weaker?
options: Because a collision document naturally contains real technical keywords across many topics, so it wins on both semantic search AND keyword search simultaneously, giving two independent chances of retrieval
Because hybrid retrieval only checks keyword matches, ignoring semantic meaning entirely
Because collision documents are always smaller in file size than normal documents
Because hybrid retrieval disables all input filters automatically
questions.explanation: Since a collision document genuinely discusses many topics using real terminology, it matches both retrieval methods independently, doubling its chances of surfacing for almost any query.

questions.q: In building a collision document, why should the malicious instruction be kept fairly short (roughly 20-40 words) and placed in the middle of a section?
options: Because longer instructions are always automatically rejected by embedding models
Because short instructions load faster in the vector database UI
To avoid the instruction being cut in half if it falls right on a chunk boundary during ingestion, which would make it look broken and reduce retrieval reliability
Because chunk boundaries only exist for documents longer than 10,000 words
questions.explanation: Chunking splits documents at fixed intervals; placing the payload centrally and keeping it short reduces the risk of it being fragmented across a chunk boundary.

questions.q: Which Python library is commonly used to programmatically generate a multi-section poisoned PDF document for an embedding collision attack?
options: fpdf (via the FPDF class)
matplotlib
numpy
flask
questions.explanation: The fpdf library's FPDF class is a standard way to construct and output a multi-section PDF document programmatically.

questions.q: What is described as a strong warning sign that a document might be an embedding collision attack?
options: A document that's unusually broad, touching VPN, databases, cloud, and passwords all within a single file, since most genuine documents stay focused on one topic
A document with a very short filename
A document uploaded during business hours
A document written entirely in bullet-point format
questions.explanation: Genuine documents are typically topic-focused; a single file spanning many unrelated technical domains is itself a red flag worth investigating.

questions.q: What is 'retrieval hijacking,' also known as context injection?
options: A denial-of-service attack against the embedding model's API
Uploading a document containing instructions, then triggering a query that causes the system to retrieve it so the model reads and follows those instructions inside its trusted context
A technique for stealing vector database credentials directly
A method for deleting an entire knowledge base remotely
questions.explanation: Retrieval hijacking plants instructions in a document, triggered via a chosen query, causing the model to read and follow them as trusted context — targeting the model and its tools, not just users.

questions.q: What is the key difference between retrieval hijacking and the earlier attacks (extraction, poisoning, collision) in terms of trigger strategy?
options: Retrieval hijacking specifically requires the most popular possible query for maximum impact
Retrieval hijacking wants a unique, private trigger phrase only the attacker knows, so the document stays dormant and doesn't get accidentally triggered by ordinary users
Retrieval hijacking only works against systems with no vector database
Retrieval hijacking cannot use any document upload mechanism at all
questions.explanation: Unlike collision/poisoning which seek maximum reach, hijacking deliberately uses an obscure, private trigger phrase to remain dormant until the attacker deliberately activates it.

questions.q: Why is the existence of two different trust levels (filtered user input vs. unfiltered retrieved context) considered a central concept in RAG security?
options: Most RAG systems filter direct user input but apply no filter at all to retrieved context, since that context is considered 'trusted' by default — this asymmetry is exactly what hijacking exploits
Because vector databases always use two different encryption keys
Because retrieval always happens twice for redundancy
Because this concept only applies to systems using more than one embedding model
questions.explanation: The core insight is that identical text is treated very differently depending on its source — filtered when typed by a user, but unfiltered when arriving via retrieved 'trusted' context — which is exactly the gap retrieval hijacking exploits.

questions.q: In the retrieval hijacking testing methodology, what is a 'significant tell' that a file-read tool actually exists when probing an AI system?
options: The AI responding with a completely blank message
The AI immediately crashing the server
A specific refusal about a particular file (e.g. 'Access to passwd files is restricted'), rather than a generic 'I can't help with that'
The AI asking the user for their password directly
questions.explanation: A specific, targeted refusal about one exact file path reveals that a file-read capability genuinely exists and that path specifically is blocked, unlike a vague generic refusal.

questions.q: An attacker plants a document titled 'vacation.txt' with vacation-related content plus a hidden instruction to read /etc/passwd. Why choose an off-topic cover subject like vacation destinations?
options: Because vacation-themed documents are automatically exempt from all security filters
Because vacation-related keywords always score highest in BM25 ranking
Because off-topic content is required by the vector database's file format
To ensure the document won't collide with real employee questions, so it's only retrieved when the attacker deliberately asks about that specific off-topic subject
questions.explanation: An off-topic trigger ensures the malicious document stays dormant and isn't accidentally retrieved by normal, unrelated employee queries, keeping the payload hidden until deliberately activated.

questions.q: Why should an attacker read large files in batches (specific line ranges) rather than all at once during retrieval hijacking escalation?
options: Because a file's contents added on top of retrieved chunks, system prompt, and question can overflow the context window, causing inference servers like vLLM to abort the request
Because single large reads always trigger a permanent IP ban
Because reading files in batches is required by copyright law
Because batch reading automatically encrypts the stolen data
questions.explanation: Context window limits mean a large file added to an already-full prompt can overflow the model's capacity, causing the request to be aborted — batching avoids this.

questions.q: What is the recommended architectural fix for retrieval hijacking?
options: Clearly mark retrieved content as reference data only within the prompt, and never let it directly drive privileged tool actions without re-validation
Increase the context window to an unlimited size
Disable the vector database entirely and rely only on training data
Allow retrieved content unrestricted access to all tool calls for convenience
questions.explanation: Explicitly separating retrieved data from instructions, and re-validating tool arguments regardless of their source, closes the gap that retrieval hijacking exploits.

questions.q: What is 'substitution' as an output-filter evasion technique?
options: Changing the form of data (e.g. replacing '@' with '[at]') so a static filter's exact pattern match misses it entirely
Sending the response over a different network protocol
Deleting the response and generating a new one
Encrypting the entire response with a public key
questions.explanation: Substitution alters the textual form of sensitive data just enough that a pattern-matching filter (like a regex for '@') no longer recognizes it, while a human/model can still interpret it.

questions.q: What is a zero-width space (U+200B) used for in the evasion techniques described?
options: Inserting it between every character of a flagged string so it becomes invisible to a human but breaks an exact-string filter's match
Encrypting text using a symmetric key algorithm
Compressing large files before upload
Marking the end of a document for the parser
questions.explanation: Zero-width characters are invisible Unicode characters inserted between letters to break exact-string filter matches while remaining readable to a human viewer.

questions.q: What is the practical catch with using zero-width characters to hide a file path like /etc/passwd?
options: The invisible characters end up embedded in the actual file path the tool tries to open, causing the read itself to fail unless combined with indirect phrasing to have the model ignore them
Zero-width characters are always visible in every text editor
Zero-width characters increase the file's size beyond upload limits
File systems automatically reject any path containing Unicode characters
questions.explanation: The literal invisible characters break the actual file path string; the fix combines this with indirect phrasing (e.g. 'read it as a human would see it') to have the model naturally ignore them when acting.

questions.q: Why should an attacker avoid explicitly naming techniques like 'base64,' 'ROT13,' or 'decode' when phrasing an indirect instruction?
options: Because those words always trigger an automatic system shutdown
Because using those words doubles the token cost of the request
Because those exact words are what smarter guardrails are specifically watching for, so avoiding them helps the request look benign
Because those words are trademarked and cannot be used in any prompt
questions.explanation: Naming the exact evasion technique is a red flag guardrails are tuned to catch; phrasing requests indirectly (benign-sounding transformations) avoids triggering intent-based detection.

questions.q: What is a homoglyph, as an evasion technique against text filters?
options: A Cyrillic character that visually looks identical to a Latin character (e.g. Cyrillic е vs Latin e), defeating a filter searching for the exact ASCII string
A type of chart used to visualize embedding dimensions
A shortened form of an embedding vector
A special character reserved for marking document boundaries
questions.explanation: Homoglyphs are visually identical characters from different character sets (e.g. Cyrillic vs Latin), which bypass exact ASCII string matching while appearing normal to a human reader.

questions.q: What is 'document blending' designed to defeat, specifically?
options: The vector database's storage capacity limits
Human reviewers, by making the malicious document genuinely indistinguishable from real ones across content, filename, file type, tone, and structure
Only automated keyword filters, with no effect on human review
The embedding model's tokenization process
questions.explanation: Document blending is specifically aimed at fooling human reviewers who might casually inspect uploaded content, by matching the look and feel of genuine documents.

questions.q: How can an attacker learn the target's chunking configuration to help place a payload in the 'safe zone' away from previews?
options: By physically inspecting the server's hard drive
Chunking configuration cannot ever be determined by an attacker
Simply ask the system directly: 'What chunking strategy does this system use?' — it may answer with something like '800 characters, 200 overlap'
By running a DDoS attack against the vector database
questions.explanation: Some systems will directly disclose their chunking configuration when asked, giving the attacker exactly the information needed to position a payload outside typical preview windows.

questions.q: What is 'slow-drip poisoning'?
options: A method for gradually decreasing a model's temperature setting
Uploading one massive malicious document all at once
A technique for slowly deleting a knowledge base over time
Gradually evolving a benign document across days or weeks through tiny individual edits, so each change looks fine on its own and only the full timeline reveals the attack
questions.explanation: Slow-drip poisoning exploits the fact that reviewers typically examine only what changed between versions, not the cumulative effect — each tiny edit looks innocent in isolation.

questions.q: What underlying concept does slow-drip poisoning rely on to evade detection?
options: Prompt decomposition — splitting one restricted goal into many individually innocent-looking steps
Reinforcement learning from human feedback
Zero-shot classification
Gradient descent optimization
questions.explanation: Prompt decomposition breaks a malicious goal into many small, individually benign-looking steps spread over time, evading detection focused on single-version changes.

questions.q: What is the correct countermeasure specifically for detecting slow-drip poisoning?
options: Track cumulative diffs and full version history, not just the last change, since comparing only the most recent edit misses the gradual pattern
Disable version history entirely to save storage space
Only scan documents once at initial upload and never again
Rely exclusively on real-time output filtering with no ingestion-side review
questions.explanation: Since each individual edit looks benign, only reviewing the full cumulative timeline of changes reveals the gradual, coordinated pattern of a slow-drip attack.

questions.q: What is 'multi-modal camouflage' as an evasion technique?
options: Hiding instructions inside images (read via OCR) or PDF metadata, where the model parses them but a human simply sees an innocent picture or clean document
A technique for converting text into multiple languages simultaneously
A method for compressing video files before upload
A defense mechanism that blocks all non-text file uploads
questions.explanation: Multi-modal camouflage exploits the gap between what a model actually parses (e.g. OCR text in an image) and what a human visually perceives (an innocuous picture).

questions.q: What is 'event fatigue' as an evasion angle?
options: A technique for making the model refuse all requests after too many events
A method for automatically archiving old documents
Flooding the system with a large volume of benign events so real, meaningful changes hide within the resulting noise, overwhelming reviewers and automated scanners
A bug that causes the vector database to crash under high load
questions.explanation: Event fatigue overwhelms both human and automated review capacity with volume, making it harder to notice the specific malicious changes buried within the noise.

questions.q: What is the guiding principle behind almost every meaningful RAG defense?
options: Treat retrieved content as untrusted data, and tightly control who can read or write to the knowledge base
Rely exclusively on the system prompt for all security enforcement
Disable retrieval entirely and use only the model's training data
Trust all retrieved content by default since it comes from an internal source
questions.explanation: The two core principles — treating retrieved content as untrusted, and controlling knowledge base access — underpin nearly every defense in RAG security.

questions.q: What is 'least privilege' as applied to a RAG service's infrastructure?
options: The RAG service should always run with full administrator/root access for reliability
Least privilege only applies to human users, never to automated services
The RAG service should have unlimited access to all company systems by default
The RAG service should run as a low-privilege user, with its file-read or web-request tools tightly scoped to only what's necessary
questions.explanation: Least privilege restricts the RAG service's own system permissions and tool scope to the minimum necessary, limiting the damage a successful attack (like retrieval hijacking) could cause.

questions.q: A retrieval function only returns a chunk to the model if `user.clearance >= chunk.metadata["required_clearance"]` AND the chunk is not tagged `is_secret`. What two conditions does this enforce?
options: The user's clearance must meet or exceed the chunk's required clearance, AND the chunk must not be tagged as a secret
The chunk must contain at least one number and one special character
The chunk must be written in English and be shorter than 100 words
The chunk must have been uploaded within the last 24 hours
questions.explanation: This access-control pattern checks both the caller's clearance level against the chunk's required clearance metadata, and explicitly excludes chunks flagged as secrets.

questions.q: Why does the example normalize_text() function strip characters where unicodedata.category(ch)[0] == 'C'?
options: Because category 'C' only appears in corrupted or malformed files
Because category 'C' marks characters that are too computationally expensive to process
Because category 'C' represents all characters in the Cyrillic alphabet specifically
Because category 'C' represents control/format characters, including zero-width and invisible characters used to hide malicious instructions
questions.explanation: Unicode category 'C' covers control and format characters, including zero-width spaces — stripping these defeats invisible-character-based evasion techniques.

questions.q: What is the correct fix for redaction that only checks for a literal '@' character to catch email addresses?
options: Disable all output filtering entirely
Redact based on meaning, not just format — use entity recognition instead, and validate the final rendered output
Increase the model's context window size
Only redact emails that end in .com specifically
questions.explanation: Format-only redaction (like matching '@') is trivially bypassed via substitution; meaning-based entity recognition is a more robust approach, per the best-practices checklist.

questions.q: What anomaly signal in the detection table specifically points to a likely embedding collision attack?
options: A user asking two unrelated questions in the same session
A document uploaded outside business hours
One document matching many unrelated query clusters
A single failed login attempt
questions.explanation: The defenses lesson's anomaly table specifically flags 'one document matching many unrelated query clusters' as the tell-tale signature of an embedding collision attack.

questions.q: What anomaly signal specifically points to likely retrieval hijacking, per the detection table?
options: A document written in a language other than English
A user changing their password twice in one week
A tool call to a sensitive path originating from retrieved context
An unusually large number of PDF uploads on a single day
questions.explanation: A tool call to a sensitive path triggered by retrieved (not directly typed) context is the specific signal indicating retrieval hijacking is occurring.

questions.q: Why are guardrails (input/output filters) considered necessary but not sufficient for RAG security on their own?
options: Input and output filters catch obvious/lazy attacks but don't reliably stop encoding tricks, indirect instructions, or trusted-context injection on their own — real security requires layered architecture
Guardrails are entirely optional and provide zero security value
Guardrails only function during the ingestion phase, never during retrieval
Guardrails require a paid license to be effective
questions.explanation: Guardrails handle the obvious cases but are insufficient alone against sophisticated evasion; real security requires access control, data-instruction separation, least privilege, and monitoring layered together.

questions.q: What is the recommended mental model for thinking about a RAG system's knowledge base from a security standpoint?
options: The knowledge base should always be treated as 100% trustworthy since it's internal company data
The knowledge base is an input, not a source of truth — every chunk could theoretically have been written by an attacker
The knowledge base is equivalent to the model's own training data in trust level
The knowledge base only needs security review if it exceeds 1,000 documents
questions.explanation: Treating the knowledge base as an input rather than an inherently trustworthy source of truth is the mental model that undercuts most RAG attacks.

questions.q: What is listed as the top cause of poisoning attacks in the ingestion best practices?
options: Storing metadata in PostgreSQL instead of MongoDB
Setting Top-K too low
Anonymous or fully open document uploads
Using too many embedding dimensions
questions.explanation: Unrestricted, anonymous upload access is explicitly identified as the top cause of poisoning attacks, making authentication and role-based upload restriction the key mitigation.

questions.q: When testing a real RAG system, what is a sound methodology order to follow?
options: Fingerprint, extract, map capabilities, poison (if in scope), hijack, evade, report
Report first, then poison, then fingerprint last
Hijack immediately without any prior reconnaissance
Evade detection before confirming the system is even RAG-based
questions.explanation: A sound methodology starts with confirming RAG usage, then progresses through extraction, capability mapping, poisoning, hijacking, evasion, and finally reporting.

questions.q: A tester confirms a chatbot exists by seeing 'Powered by RAG' branding and an upload feature. What should be their next logical testing step?
options: Extract — probe for sensitive data using precise, 'include all' style prompts and one-shot examples
Immediately attempt retrieval hijacking without any further recon
Skip directly to writing the final report
Delete a random document to test permissions
questions.explanation: After fingerprinting confirms the system is RAG-based, the next methodology step is information extraction using precise, completeness-demanding prompts.

questions.q: A defender implements per-chunk access control and Unicode normalization but does NOT separate retrieved data from instructions in the prompt. Which specific attack class remains largely unaddressed?
options: Retrieval hijacking, since the model can still treat retrieved text as trusted commands even with proper access control and normalization in place
Information extraction, which is already fully solved by access control alone
SQL injection, which is unrelated to any RAG-specific defense
Embedding collision, which cannot occur once Unicode is normalized
questions.explanation: Access control governs WHO can retrieve WHAT, and normalization defeats certain encoding tricks — but without explicitly marking retrieved content as data-only, the model can still follow embedded instructions, leaving hijacking unaddressed.

questions.q: Why is 'monitoring previews only, not full documents' listed as a mistake that lets document blending succeed?
options: Because monitoring tools typically display truncated chunk excerpts, so content hidden deeper within a chunk (in the 'safe zone') never actually appears in the preview a reviewer sees
Because document blending only works on documents with no preview feature at all
Because previews are always encrypted and cannot be read by security teams
Because monitoring previews consume too much server bandwidth to be practical
questions.explanation: Document blending specifically exploits the gap between preview-based review (truncated excerpts) and full document content, hiding payloads outside what a preview actually shows.

questions.q: What combination of defenses would most directly counter a well-executed embedding collision attack that also uses slow-drip techniques?
options: Disabling semantic search entirely while keeping keyword search active
Relying solely on an output filter that checks for the '@' character
Only checking the most recent single edit to each document
Flagging documents matching abnormally wide query clusters, plus tracking cumulative version history rather than just the latest change
questions.explanation: Since a combined collision+slow-drip attack starts broad and evolves gradually, catching it requires both breadth-anomaly detection (unusual topic spread) and cumulative diff tracking, not either alone.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the sentence_transformers library and cosine similarity technique in both the ingestion poisoning and embedding collision lessons?
options: To automatically generate malicious payloads without human input
To directly modify the production vector database in real time
To encrypt documents before they are uploaded to the knowledge base
To allow an attacker (or defender) to test offline how closely a candidate document's embedding matches various target queries, before ever uploading the real file
questions.explanation: Both lessons use sentence_transformers and cosine similarity to test and refine a document's retrieval likelihood offline, iterating before committing to an actual upload.

questions.q: What does BM25 primarily use to score how relevant a chunk is to a search query?
options: The chunk's file creation timestamp
The presence and frequency of the query's exact search terms within the chunk, especially rarer terms
The total number of images embedded in the chunk
The chunk's alphabetical position in the document
questions.explanation: BM25 scores chunks higher based on the presence and frequency of matching search terms, particularly rarer/more distinctive terms.

questions.q: What is a vector database used for in a RAG pipeline?
options: Managing user login credentials for the chatbot
Storing only plain, unstructured text with no search capability
Running the LLM's inference computations directly
Storing embeddings and quickly finding the ones nearest to a given query vector
questions.explanation: A vector database is purpose-built to store embeddings and perform fast nearest-neighbor (similarity) search across them.

questions.q: In the retrieval hijacking escalation example, what is the purpose of matching the UID from /proc/self/status against /etc/passwd contents?
options: To permanently delete the RAG service's account
To determine exactly which user account the RAG service is running as, revealing its actual privilege level
To automatically generate a new SSH key pair
To encrypt the stolen data before exfiltration
questions.explanation: Cross-referencing the running process's UID against the password file reveals the service account's identity and privilege level, informing further escalation potential.

questions.q: Why is administrators over-provisioning a RAG service's privileges a significant real-world risk?
options: Best practice calls for a low-privilege service account, but if over-provisioned, a successful retrieval hijacking attack could access far more than intended
Because over-provisioning always causes the vector database to run out of storage immediately
Because over-provisioning is required by most compliance frameworks
Because over-provisioning has no security implications whatsoever, only performance ones
questions.explanation: If the RAG service runs with more privileges than necessary, a successful retrieval hijacking attack can leverage those excess privileges for much greater impact than intended.

questions.q: A RAG system uses hybrid retrieval with re-ranking, per-chunk access control, and treats retrieved content as data-only in the prompt. Which combination of attack techniques would a red teamer most reasonably prioritize testing first?
options: Embedding collision combined with slow-drip poisoning and careful chunk-boundary placement, since these specifically target detection gaps (broad-topic anomaly evasion and cumulative-change blindness) rather than the already-hardened access-control and data/instruction separation layers
A basic 'ignore previous instructions' payload sent directly as a user message, since prompt engineering alone bypasses all RAG-specific defenses
SQL injection against the vector database's REST API, since vector databases are always vulnerable to classic SQL injection
Nothing further can be tested since all listed defenses are already fully comprehensive
questions.explanation: Since access control and data/instruction separation are already addressed, an attacker would logically pivot to techniques that specifically target the remaining gaps: detection evasion via broad topical coverage and gradual, cumulative changes.

questions.q: Why does combining paraphrase spreading (from ingestion poisoning) with the embedding collision technique make an attack particularly resistant to exact-phrase security reviews?
options: Because reworded content is always shorter and therefore skipped by scanners looking for long text
Because rewording the malicious instruction slightly in each section/file means a review searching for one exact phrase across documents will miss all the reworded copies entirely
Because paraphrasing automatically encrypts the malicious content using a random cipher
Because paraphrase spreading disables the vector database's indexing capability entirely
questions.explanation: Exact-phrase-matching security reviews are specifically defeated by rewording each instance of the malicious content, since no single searchable string appears identically across all planted copies.

questions.q: Why is comparing the LAST change alone (rather than the full cumulative diff history) insufficient for catching slow-drip poisoning?
options: Because comparing changes requires more storage than the entire vector database itself
Because each individual tiny edit looks perfectly fine on its own, and only the full timeline of changes actually reveals the coordinated malicious pattern
Because the last change is always encrypted and cannot be inspected
Because the last change is always identical to the first change by design
questions.explanation: Slow-drip poisoning is specifically designed so each individual step looks innocuous — only reviewing the cumulative history across all versions reveals the underlying malicious trajectory.

questions.q: What is the consequence of a RAG defense that filters user input but does not filter retrieved context?
options: Retrieval hijacking becomes possible, since instructions hidden in retrieved documents bypass the input filter entirely
The vector database automatically becomes read-only
Embedding dimensions are permanently reduced to zero
The system automatically switches to keyword-only search
questions.explanation: Filtering only direct user input while leaving retrieved context unfiltered is exactly the gap retrieval hijacking exploits.

questions.q: What is the consequence of 'trusting guardrails alone,' per the common mistakes table?
options: Encoding and indirect prompts slip through, since guardrails alone don't catch every evasion technique
All retrieved chunks are permanently deleted after each query
The system becomes completely immune to all forms of attack
The vector database automatically encrypts itself
questions.explanation: Guardrails alone are insufficient against sophisticated evasion (encoding, indirect phrasing), which is why layered defense — not guardrails in isolation — is the recommended approach.

questions.q: In a secure RAG ingestion design, which specific metadata field would be checked to determine if a chunk should NEVER be surfaced to the chatbot, regardless of user clearance?
options: An is_secret field, explicitly tagged as True/False on each chunk
The chunk's file creation date only
The total word count of the chunk
The name of the embedding model used
questions.explanation: Explicitly filtering out any chunk where metadata.is_secret is true acts as an additional safety layer beyond clearance-based filtering.

questions.q: A tester wants to confirm an embedding collision document actually works after uploading. What is the correct verification method?
options: Ask about several completely unrelated subjects (e.g. VPN, cloud services, databases) and check whether the same hidden step appears in every single answer
Check the file's upload timestamp in the admin panel
Measure the exact byte size of the uploaded PDF file
Ask only one single question and assume success if any answer is returned at all
questions.explanation: Confirming embedding collision requires testing multiple genuinely unrelated topics and checking that the same hidden instruction rides along in each response, proving broad retrieval coverage.

questions.q: What is the key structural reason a 'collision document' is more efficient for an attacker than deploying several separate single-topic poisoned documents?
options: Collision documents automatically bypass every possible defense with zero effort
A single artifact is easier to manage, update, and later remove, while still achieving the broad multi-topic reach that would otherwise require several separate ingestion-poisoning documents
Separate documents are always technically impossible to upload to any RAG system
Collision documents require no recon of any kind, unlike any other RAG attack
questions.explanation: The efficiency benefit is operational: one file achieving broad coverage is simpler to manage and clean up than maintaining multiple separate poisoned documents targeting individual topics.

questions.q: Which combination of tools/techniques would be most appropriate for a red teamer testing whether a target RAG system's output filter can be bypassed for leaking email addresses?
options: Use nmap to scan the RAG application's open ports
Request the output with a substitution transformation (e.g. replacing '@' with '[at]') to defeat a likely regex-based redaction filter
Send a malformed HTTP request designed to crash the inference server
Attempt a brute-force password attack against the vector database directly
questions.explanation: Substitution is the specific technique demonstrated in the lesson for bypassing regex-based output filters looking for an exact pattern like '@'.

questions.q: Why are access-controlled ingestion AND treating retrieved content as untrusted on output BOTH necessary, rather than just one or the other?
options: Access control alone doesn't stop a poisoned or hijacked document from being treated as trusted once retrieved, and treating output as untrusted alone doesn't stop unauthorized ingestion in the first place — both ends of the pipeline need protection
Only one of the two is actually necessary and the other is purely optional
Access control and output handling are actually the exact same technical mechanism
These two principles only apply to systems using semantic search, never keyword search
questions.explanation: The two principles address different pipeline stages — who can get content IN, and how content is treated once retrieved OUT — and a gap in either one leaves a meaningful attack surface open.

questions.q: An attacker tests a candidate embedding-collision document offline and finds a low cosine similarity score against one specific target query. What should the attacker do next?
options: Rewrite that section of the document to incorporate more of that query's actual words/terminology, then re-test
Delete the test query from the list and ignore that topic entirely
Immediately abandon the entire collision document attempt
Increase the embedding model's temperature setting
questions.explanation: A low similarity score signals that section needs more relevant keywords and detail matching that query's phrasing — the attacker iterates and re-tests, similar to SEO-style optimization.

questions.q: A defender notices the same verification URL appearing across documents about VPN, cloud access, and database connections — three unrelated topics. What attack does this most strongly suggest?
options: Embedding collision, since the anomaly table specifically flags identical instructions/URLs appearing across many unrelated topics as a warning sign
A normal software license key shared across departments
A legitimate company-wide security policy update with no attack involved
A DNS misconfiguration unrelated to the RAG system
questions.explanation: The same suspicious URL/instruction appearing across genuinely unrelated topics is the exact signature the defenses lesson identifies as indicating an embedding collision or ingestion poisoning attack.

questions.q: What does the phrase 'defense in depth' mean as applied to RAG security?
options: No single control (access control, guardrails, normalization, monitoring) is ever enough on its own — real security comes from layering multiple defenses together
Relying entirely on the single strongest available defense while ignoring the rest
Physically locking the server room as the only necessary security measure
Using the deepest possible neural network architecture for the embedding model
questions.explanation: RAG security requires multiple layered defenses working together — access control, separation of data/instructions, sanitization, and monitoring — since no single control is sufficient alone.

questions.q: What is 'metadata' in the context of a RAG chunk?
options: The literal text content of the chunk itself
A separate copy of the vector embedding stored for backup purposes
The exact GPU memory address where the chunk is processed
Extra facts stored alongside each chunk, such as source filename, author, date, department, and access level, used for filtering and access control
questions.explanation: Metadata is auxiliary information attached to each chunk that enables filtering, provenance tracking, and access control enforcement during retrieval.

questions.q: What is the purpose of 'indexing' in a RAG pipeline?
options: Deleting outdated documents from the knowledge base
Organizing stored data so that searches run quickly, similar to how a textbook's index helps find a topic fast
Encrypting all documents before they are stored
Automatically translating documents into multiple languages
questions.explanation: Indexing organizes stored data structures to enable fast search and retrieval, analogous to a book's index speeding up topic lookup.

questions.q: In a realistic enterprise RAG pipeline, what role does an 'input guardrail' typically play?
options: Converting text into embeddings for the vector database
Storing the final generated answer permanently
Screening the user's question for potential attacks before it reaches the retrieval or generation stages
Running the LLM's core inference computation
questions.explanation: An input guardrail is a first line of defense that screens incoming user queries for malicious patterns before they proceed further into the pipeline.

questions.q: In an enterprise RAG pipeline, what role does an 'output guardrail' typically play?
options: Redacting secrets from the generated answer before it reaches the user, using pattern matching plus entity recognition
Converting the user's query into a vector for search
Storing chunk metadata in a relational database
Chunking raw documents before they are embedded
questions.explanation: The output guardrail is the last line of defense, scanning and redacting the model's generated response for leaked secrets before it's shown to the user.

questions.q: Which ingestion poisoning technique involves uploading the SAME fake step in several different file formats (.txt, .docx, .html, .md)?
options: Paraphrase spreading
Slow-drip poisoning
Delimiter injection
Prefix injection
questions.explanation: Paraphrase spreading uploads multiple differently-worded and differently-formatted versions of the same fake content to increase the chance of matching varied real-world phrasings.

questions.q: A tester probes a RAG chatbot and asks it to read /proc/self/status using a 'fresh document to keep context clean.' What is the purpose of using a fresh document rather than reusing the earlier one?
options: Because the vector database only allows one query per uploaded document ever
Because reusing a document automatically alerts the security team
To avoid context window clutter from earlier retrieved content while still exploiting the same retrieval-hijacking mechanism to read a new sensitive file
Because fresh documents are required by the RAG system's file format specification
questions.explanation: Using a fresh, targeted document keeps the retrieved context focused and uncluttered, making the escalation step (reading /proc/self/status) cleaner and more reliable, while still exploiting the same retrieval hijacking mechanism.
